name: Cat-eye surgery (canthal tilt lift)

lead: Canthal tilt is the angle between the inner and outer corners of the eye. Looksmaxxing communities treat an upward outer corner as a desirable feature, and cat-eye surgery aims to lift the lateral canthus to produce it.
It belongs to the family of canthoplasty, plastic surgery of the corner of the eye, which is used both cosmetically and to fix eyelid position or function.

paras: The procedure is done by a surgeon on the outer corner of the eyelids, usually as an outpatient operation under local anesthesia. Specifics vary by surgeon and technique; this wiki gives no step-by-step details. Recovery and swelling are discussed with the operating surgeon.
As eyelid surgery, it carries risks to eyelid position and eye surface, and results depend on the surgeon. Candidates should consult a qualified oculoplastic or plastic surgeon.

angle.text: The procedure changes the position of the outer eye corner so the eye slants upward and looks more elongated. People pursue it to change the shape of the eye area.

lead: Cat-eye surgery, or canthal tilt lift, is a cosmetic procedure aimed at raising the outer corner of the eye to give a more upward-slanting, almond-shaped look with a "positive" canthal tilt. People who choose it do so to change how the eye area reads in the face: a lifted outer corner is the feature they are after. [1][2]

Clinically the procedures involved are lateral canthoplasty and canthopexy, forms of canthoplasty, which Wikipedia describes as plastic surgery of the medial and/or lateral canthus used in cosmetic work and in procedures addressing eyelid function or malposition. [1] On social media the cosmetic version is also called "fox eye" surgery, a term used by the public rather than by clinicians. [3]

Published literature on the cosmetic application consists mainly of surgeon-written technique descriptions rather than controlled studies. Surgeons' practice pages note that most canthal surgery is performed for functional reasons such as lid laxity, and that the cosmetic use is newer. [3]
infobox: Canthal tilt surgery, fox eye surgery
Roughly 30 minutes to 2 hours depending on source and combined procedures [2][4]

paras: Canthoplasty is plastic surgery of the medial and/or lateral canthus. A related procedure, canthotomy, cuts the canthus and is mainly used to relieve orbital pressure. [1]

Surgeons distinguish two main approaches for the outer corner. Canthopexy tightens and reinforces the existing canthal tendon without detaching it, and produces a more modest change. Canthoplasty detaches the lateral canthal tendon from the orbital rim, reshapes it and reattaches it in a new position, allowing a larger change at higher risk. [3][4] One consumer eye-health article describes canthopexy as not creating the slanted shape, while describing canthoplasty as the procedure that does. [2]

Cosmetic goals listed by an oculofacial surgery clinic include lifting a downward-slanting outer corner, tightening loose tissue at the outer lower lid, creating a more defined almond contour and improving asymmetry between the two sides. [4] The operation can be combined with other work such as double eyelid surgery, epicanthoplasty, fat grafting or brow lifts. [2][5]

A 2016 technique paper by Soo Wook Chae and Byung Min Yun in Archives of Plastic Surgery describes a cosmetic lateral canthoplasty done through an incision along the lateral canthal crease, release of the lateral canthal attachments and fixation of the corner to the inside of the lateral orbital wall. The authors say it lengthens the lateral canthal angle and lowers a raised outer tail of the eye, with more visible effects in eyes with double eyelids. [5]

Accounts of recovery are broadly consistent. Sutures are removed or dissolve within about a week, bruising and swelling fade over roughly one to two weeks, and most swelling resolves within a month. [2][4][5] Chae and Yun report that swelling falls by more than 90 percent by one month and that the scar can look red for two to three months. [5] The consumer article advises waiting about a month before using saunas, pools or contact lenses. [2]

Risks named by clinic and surgeon sources include bleeding or hematoma, infection, scarring at the outer corner, asymmetry, overcorrection or undercorrection that may need revision, changes in sensation, altered tear drainage or dry eye, and gradual return of laxity with age. [2][4]

A Melbourne-area surgeon's article lists asymmetry as the most common aesthetic complaint and also describes blunting or rounding of the corner, webbing, scleral show, ectropion, lid retraction, altered blink and, rarely, visual disturbance. It states that the fox-eye application is a permanent structural change, that revision is harder than the original operation and that assessment for revision is usually deferred six to twelve months. [3]

Chae and Yun list conjunctival hemorrhage and edema, which they say are usually managed without further surgery, and uncommon corneal dellen. They also describe wound separation leading to a fish-mouth scar and lower lid eversion as complications they aim to avoid. [5] The consumer article advises contacting the surgeon immediately for severe pain or a change in vision after surgery. [2]

Cosmetic canthoplasty and canthopexy are performed for appearance and are typically not covered by health insurance unless the surgery treats a medical condition. [2][4] Quoted prices vary by surgeon and location and often exclude anesthesia and facility fees. [2]

A positive canthal tilt is a commonly discussed trait in looksmaxxing communities, which is why surgical lifting is discussed there as a "hardmaxx" option, meaning a surgical rather than non-surgical route to a better-looking face.

No studies found. The closest published material is Chae and Yun's 2016 technique paper, which presents three illustrated cases without quantitative measurements, and the broader literature on canthoplasty for lid malposition and laxity. [5]

timeline.event: Chae and Yun publish a cosmetic lateral canthoplasty technique in Archives of Plastic Surgery. [5]
